title: [DECODED] Scam season and the leaks that may make it worse
summary: If recent leaks and scam warnings made you rethink your digital habits, there’s a place to start

blocks.text: If recent leaks and scam warnings made you rethink your digital habits, there’s a place to start

items: With only 37 days until Christmas, holiday preparations are causing increased traffic in Metro Manila, coinciding with the recent ASEAN Summit.
A GSMA survey reveals that while many Filipinos are aware of scams, with 76% expressing concern, scams continue to evolve, including new methods like 'quishing' via QR codes.

Recent data breaches have exposed personal information from various government agencies, prompting warnings about increased scam risks during the holiday season and highlighting the need for better public awareness and reporting mechanisms.

There are only 37 days before Christmas! Have you started your holiday preparations already, and are you feeling the Christmas rush yet? I’ve noticed that Metro Manila traffic has been heavier over the past week, although that may have been due to preparations for the 49th ASEAN Summit, which just wrapped up.

Between the traffic and the shopping, the holidays are when we’re busiest and least careful, especially with our transactions. A recent survey by the global industry trade organization GSM Association (GSMA) said that Filipinos do know the risk: 76% said they “absolutely worry” about scams and 78% said they changed their behavior due to scam awareness.

And yet, scams still proliferate — and they have been evolving along with technology. Smishing (SMS phishing) has been in the public consciousness for a while now, but have you heard of quishing? It essentially does the same thing, except that it’s done via QR codes.

Rappler researcher Lourence Angelo Marcellana listed 12 types of scams to watch out for, as we approach the holiday season. He also explained how to protect yourself against scams, especially since much of our transactions now happen online, thanks to the growth of e-commerce and digital payments.

In the GSMA report, it said that the Philippines also has the highest rate — among Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Vietnam — of reporting scams to digital platforms (49%), compared to only 16% reporting to the police. The regional average of reporting scams to the authorities is at 36%.

This reminded me of a Decoded study we did last year on online scams. We found that government agencies were among the most active sharers of warnings online, but because each agency’s approach lacked coordination with the others, the overall effect on consumers online was dissatisfaction from all the fragmented messaging.

Users online also complained about the government hotlines set up for reporting scams, saying that they found them difficult to use and lacking a clear process to submit evidence and receive updates on their cases.
That was last year. This year, the problem has now moved from how well the public is warned to knowing what kind of personal details may already be exposed, and who might be using them.

Last Friday, November 13, the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) confirmed that personal data from around 20 state agencies were exposed in recent data breaches. Rappler researcher Alex Culla looked into these agencies and listed the personal information potentially exposed, from the Bureau of Internal Revenue, Securities and Exchange Commission, to the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation.

Among the personal details that may have been compromised are names, addresses, email addresses, mobile numbers, birth dates, genders, and even taxpayer identification numbers (TIN). Of course, these vary depending on the agency, and not everyone who deals with these agencies is necessarily affected. But it’s still worth staying alert, because while scams do happen all year, the CICC said it might become more prevalent as the holidays approach.
So if these recent leaks and scam warnings made you rethink your digital habits, there’s a place to start. At Rappler, Christmas isn’t the only thing we’re counting down to.

This year’s Social Good Summit is taking place this Saturday, November 21, and it will include a masterclass on data privacy and personal safety in the age of AI. There will also be discussions on technology, journalism, and human rights, as well as masterclasses on vibe coding, editorial cartooning, and crisis management.
